title: Sleep Hygiene: Building Habits for Restful Sleep
content:
Adults need 7–9 hours of sleep per night, according to the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the CDC. Teenagers need 8–10 hours, and school-age children need 9–12 hours. Consistently getting less than the recommended amount is linked to increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and mental health problems.

Sleep hygiene refers to a set of behavioural and environmental practices that promote consistent, quality sleep. The most evidence-backed habits include:

Keep a consistent schedule. Going to bed and waking at the same time every day — including weekends — anchors your body's internal clock (circadian rhythm) and makes it easier to fall asleep and wake naturally.

Make the bedroom dark, quiet, and cool. Core body temperature needs to drop slightly to initiate sleep; a room temperature between 15–19 degrees Celsius (60–67 degrees Fahrenheit) suits most people. Blackout curtains or a sleep mask help block light, which suppresses melatonin production.

Limit screens before bed. Blue-spectrum light from phones, tablets, and computer monitors suppresses melatonin. Avoiding screens for 30–60 minutes before bedtime, or using night-mode settings, can help.

Avoid caffeine in the afternoon and evening. Caffeine has a half-life of roughly five to six hours; a coffee at 4 PM may still have half its caffeine in your system at 9–10 PM.

Use the bed only for sleep and sex. Doing work or watching television in bed trains the brain to associate the bed with wakefulness rather than sleep.

If you cannot fall asleep after 20 minutes, get up and do a calm, non-screen activity (such as reading a physical book) in dim light until you feel sleepy again.

Persistent insomnia lasting more than three months should be evaluated by a healthcare provider. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is recommended as the first-line treatment before sleep medications for chronic insomnia.
source: Original — based on CDC Sleep and Sleep Disorders guidance (public domain) and AASM consensus recommendations
